Chapter 30

Remote functions

query, command and form from $app/server — what replaces most of an API, and the one job left for a real endpoint.

By the end of this chapter

Call the server as if it were a function, with validation, CSRF and types for free.

Tessera has exactly two API routes. Everything else that would have been an endpoint is a remote function: an async function you export from a .remote.ts file and *import into a component*, where calling it performs a typed, validated, CSRF-protected request.

Three things without any code: the payload is validated by the same valibot schema the client imports, the CSRF origin check runs, and the call is typed end to end — so a change to PushSchema breaks the caller at build time rather than at runtime in production.

A refusal is data, not a crash

The client has already applied these operations locally — that is what local-first means — so it needs a status it can *act on*. 403 means "stop and reload". 422 means "your clock is wrong and this will keep happening". A 500 would tell it to retry forever, which for a permanent failure is a client that hammers the server until the tab closes. The IngestError → error(status, message) translation is three lines and it is what makes #onPushFailure in chapter 24 able to distinguish retryable from not.

query

Note how little it does. It reads a row and returns it. It does not replay operations, build a document, or hold a CRDT in memory — the client streams everything after that sequence and applies it itself, which it has to be able to do anyway because that is the same path every subsequent edit takes.

The alternative — a server that materialises the current state on every open — looks tidier and gives the server an opinion about the document, which then has to agree with the client’s opinion forever. When two authorities disagree about a CRDT, the one with the database usually wins, and the user’s unsynced work is what loses.

Returning something with behaviour

openBoard returns a LoadedBoard, which is a *class*. That works because of the transport hook, and it is worth seeing what it buys.

Read the warning at the top of that block before adding an entry of your own. SvelteKit serialises with devalue, which already handles Date, Map, Set, RegExp, BigInt, URL, Infinity, NaN, -0 and cyclic references. Most reaching for transport is unnecessary, and every unnecessary entry is a pair of functions that can drift apart. Both entries here carry behaviour, which is the thing devalue genuinely cannot reconstruct.

The payoff: the browser gets an object that can hydrate() itself into a reactive document. The alternative is every call site doing BoardDocument.fromSnapshot(actorId(), result.snapshot) and one of them eventually forgetting the actor — which, per chapter 21, is a bug that presents as typing occasionally vanishing.

What is left for a real endpoint

  • /api/boards/[board]/stream — a GET that never ends. A remote function returns a value; this returns a ReadableStream that stays open for hours.
  • /api/boards/[board]/snapshot — a document, fetched by an embedded custom element on somebody else’s page, which has no SvelteKit client to call a remote function with.

That is a useful rule of thumb for the whole feature: a remote function replaces a request/response endpoint. It does not replace a stream or a public document.

Checkpoint

  • You can call the server from a component with no fetch, no route and no manual types.
  • Changing a schema breaks the caller at build time.
  • You can name the two things a remote function is not for.
